Potions: A Curious Tale is a fantasy adventure game developed and published by Stumbling Cat that combines potion crafting, exploration, puzzle-solving, and light combat into a charming and highly creative experience. Instead of focusing primarily on swordplay or traditional RPG combat systems, the game builds its entire identity around magical experimentation and clever problem-solving. This approach gives the adventure a refreshing personality that separates it from many other fantasy games, creating an experience that feels relaxing, imaginative, and consistently rewarding for players who enjoy exploration and creativity.

The story follows Luna, a young aspiring witch who leaves home to continue learning the art of potion brewing while uncovering mysteries hidden throughout a magical world. The narrative embraces a warm and whimsical tone from beginning to end, presenting an adventure centered around curiosity and discovery rather than dark drama or large-scale conflict. Luna quickly becomes an appealing protagonist because of her enthusiasm and determination, and her journey through enchanted forests, mysterious ruins, and dangerous landscapes captures the feeling of a magical storybook brought to life.

One of the game’s strongest features is how deeply integrated the potion system is within every aspect of gameplay. Potions are not simply consumable healing items or temporary stat boosts. Instead, they function as the primary tools players use to interact with the world itself. Different brews can freeze enemies, ignite obstacles, create explosions, manipulate environmental hazards, or solve puzzles in creative ways. This mechanic constantly encourages experimentation because players are rewarded for thinking creatively rather than simply relying on brute force. Many challenges can be approached using multiple potion combinations, making progression feel flexible and inventive.

Exploration plays a major role throughout the adventure and consistently feels rewarding because the world is filled with useful ingredients, hidden treasures, and environmental secrets. Every new area introduces additional resources and opportunities to discover stronger recipes or alternate solutions to obstacles. Gathering ingredients becomes an enjoyable part of the gameplay loop because crafting directly impacts progression and puzzle-solving. Searching forests, caves, beaches, and ancient ruins for rare materials creates a satisfying sense of adventure while also reinforcing the game’s focus on experimentation.

The crafting system itself is surprisingly engaging despite its accessible design. As players discover new ingredients and recipes, the possibilities for experimentation steadily expand. Learning how different potion effects interact with enemies and environmental mechanics becomes one of the most satisfying aspects of the game. Certain puzzles require observation and planning rather than quick reflexes, which gives the gameplay a thoughtful pace that complements the game’s relaxed atmosphere perfectly.

Combat exists throughout the adventure, but it is intentionally designed to support the potion mechanics rather than overshadow them. Enemies can often be avoided, manipulated, or defeated through clever use of brews and environmental interactions instead of direct attacks alone. This creates encounters that feel more strategic and creative than traditional action combat. While the fighting mechanics themselves are relatively simple, the emphasis on preparation and experimentation keeps battles entertaining without turning the game into a combat-heavy experience.

Visually, Potions: A Curious Tale is filled with personality. The colorful environments, expressive animations, and whimsical fantasy designs create a world that feels warm and inviting. Character designs are charming and memorable, while each environment maintains its own visual identity through distinct colors, magical details, and lively scenery. The overall presentation resembles an interactive fantasy storybook, which fits the game’s tone and themes extremely well.

The soundtrack further enhances the cozy atmosphere with soft fantasy-inspired music that accompanies exploration without becoming repetitive or distracting. Sound effects for potion brewing, magical reactions, and environmental interactions all feel satisfying and reinforce the sense of immersion. Together, the visuals and audio create a relaxing atmosphere that makes simply exploring the world enjoyable even outside of progression and objectives.

Another major strength of the game is its pacing. New mechanics, potion types, and environmental interactions are introduced gradually, preventing the experience from becoming overwhelming. The game gives players enough freedom to experiment while still maintaining a steady sense of progression. This balance helps keep the adventure consistently engaging without relying on excessive complexity or constant combat encounters.

However, the game is not without flaws. Some quests require noticeable backtracking between previously explored areas, which can occasionally slow the pacing during longer sessions. Combat mechanics, while functional, lack the depth that players expecting a more action-focused RPG might desire. Certain puzzle solutions can also become predictable once players fully understand the available potion mechanics. Additionally, while the world and atmosphere are charming, the overall story remains relatively straightforward and may not fully satisfy players looking for a more emotionally complex narrative.

Even with those shortcomings, Potions: A Curious Tale succeeds because of how confidently it commits to its central idea of magical experimentation. Every aspect of the game revolves around creativity, discovery, and problem-solving, giving the adventure a distinct identity that feels refreshing within the fantasy genre. The game consistently rewards curiosity and clever thinking, making progression feel enjoyable rather than repetitive.

Potions: A Curious Tale ultimately stands out as a delightful and imaginative fantasy adventure that combines crafting, exploration, and puzzle-solving into a relaxing yet engaging experience. Its clever potion mechanics, colorful presentation, and satisfying progression systems create an adventure filled with charm and creativity. While it may not offer the combat complexity or narrative depth of larger RPGs, it succeeds remarkably well at delivering a magical journey driven by experimentation, curiosity, and discovery.

[h1][b] TLDR: While young kids might enjoy this game, I felt many of the mechanics and aspects of the world failed to keep me engaged.[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
✅Good travel options
✅Cozy vibe

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Artwork/Animations feel like a flash game
➖Rough UI/Controls
➖No quest log
➖Rough and potion limited combat
➖Tons of backtracking without a guide
➖Respawning enemies on zone change

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative/Length) – [3/10] [/b] [/h1]
Game World: Potions: A Curious Tale (PACT) takes place in what seems to be a sort of medieval fantasy setting. The game world takes place on smallish maze-like maps where you control your 2D sprite. There is also an overhead map where I found it incredibly convenient to travel to the exact zone I wanted to…when I actually knew where I was supposed to be going. 
The world itself is not great looking. PACT feels very much like a Flash game, and this extends to all parts of it - controls, UI, and of course the world. There are many elements like water and lava that just look like a PS1 game. 

Narrative: The narrative is pretty lighthearted, almost to the point where I’d call the protagonist naive. You play as Luna, an apprentice alchemist who has come to visit her grandmother and learn more of the craft. As you progress through the story, you meet many classic fairy tale tropes such as Snow White and Baba Yaga. 
I felt the story was just too boring and juvenile for my tastes. I am definitely not the target demographic for this game. 

Length: I made it almost to the end of the game after 3.5 hours. Therefore, I would assume the main story and some side quests to be around 5-7 hours. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [3/10] [/b] [/h1]
Mechanics: The general mechanics of PACT consist of gathering ingredients to make potions while doing your quests. There are 4 main ingredient types - fire, earth, wind, and water. You collect materials that supply a small amount of a specific type. Three ingredients then make a single potion. There must be something like 30+ potions to make. Most of the ones I made were just slightly different forms of damage or CC with some major interactions with the environment. For example, needing a fire potion to burn ice/trees, or a water potion to grow vines to climb. 
You use the various potions for simplistic combat - you just throw a potion and it does something. I found the combat to be awful. Many times I would be out of the animation for the hit, but still take damage. Also just to even engage in combat, you must use potions which cost ingredients. Adding in the fact that you must constantly make more potions and monsters respawn on zone change means that I tried to actively avoid combat. The more combat I did, the more potions I needed and more ingredients I had to have. I did not find the paltry enemy drops to be sustainable at all, so it's best to just run away from everything possible on your broom. 
I don’t like how due to some annoyances with ingredients and enemy respawns that it's better to avoid mechanics in the game. Avoiding mechanics due to the limitations of core mechanics is bad game design to me. 

Difficulty: I found the game ridiculously easy. Like the kind of challenge that Lebron James would have if he was playing high school basketball. Again, I am not the demographic for this game. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Performance) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Quality: The graphics in PACT are not the best. Kind of like a flash game. I wonder if the game has engine limitations due to things like graphical issues (lack of v-sync), bad animations, and bad backgrounds. I tried to google and see if it was a Unity game, but couldn’t find any info. Regardless, PACT does not have any graphical prowess or options to improve the game, only limit it. I also had a big issue with the UI. This screenshot says more than I can about the look and feel of PACT: 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3313430437

My one redeeming comment for this section is the artwork is just decent enough, but does appear as though its a bit simplistic and out of a children’s book. 

Performance: Aside from screen tearing issues, I had no problems running this game. 
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD

[h1] [b] Audio (Sound Effects/Music) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Sound Effects: Nothing of real note. Very simplistic. 

Music: Most of the music is forgettable. The town song did stick in my head a bit, but that might be because you’re there so often for zone swapping. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
While I didn’t finish the game, I wouldn’t give this a high mark. As far as I understand, after finishing the short ~7 hour game, the only thing left is achievements, potion combinations, and card collection puzzles. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [3/10] [/b] [/h1]
I decided to give this a 3 instead of a 2 solely for the kind developer helping people in the forums with bugs and issues. Look, I’m NOT the target demographic for this game, but I felt I should review it anyway for others that are curious (pun not intended) on what this game provides. What PACT gives you is a whimsical and simple adventure that I would have adored if I was much younger. I would recommend this to be a great game for children or even parents to play with their kids. 
It’s almost like the Hungry Caterpillar or Clifford the Big Red Dog type of storybook. Kids might love this game. Not me. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]

It's a cute game.  Manage your expectations: qualitywise, it's about on par with a long flash browser game from back in the day, aimed at 12 year olds.  Which is absolutely fine!  I'm a 40+ year old guy and rather enjoyed it :)   But understand up front that that's what you're getting.  

The music is nice and varied enough to not get tiresome.  The art is cute if limited and not always fitting.   Expect about 10 to 15 hours from start to finish.   Get this game if you like supporting truly independent developers and want something simple and cozy to spend some idle time at!  

Don't get this if you're wanting something a bit more complex and engaging or are a completionist who doesn't enjoy massive amounts of trial and error (Sometimes there are patterns, sometimes there seems to be not.  Sometimes you're just throwing every random potion type at an enemy to see how it responds.  There are no real hints, there is no real guidance beyond the mostly straightforward style of play). 

The potion crafting system is simple but functional.  There are over a hundred potions you can craft.    Aaaaaand most of them are functionally the same. Normally this wouldn't bother me, but inventory management allows you to only equip so many potions types at once and you can't change what's equipped without going to specific areas which allow you to access the rest of your supply.   

There are a great many different types of ingredients you can collect for your potions!   ...but many of them require you to use other specific types of potions to get a creature to drop the ingredient for you.  Sometimes, this is fine.  Often, it's just not worth it (or wasn't to me).  I found myself mostly just collecting whatever I could find lying around or whatever I could easily convince mobs to drop and made it through the majority of the game using only the commonly available supplies with very few exceptions. 

The majority of characters you'll meet are straight out of other stories/mythologies across multiple cultures.  If that's the kind of thing which strikes you as uninspired or lazy, you might not enjoy this one much.  Personally, I think it's fine.  Remembering that this game was made with the younger crowd in mind, it's completely fitting for almost everything to be a reference to something they've heard of or might be interested in. 

Final say: Give it a try.  Maybe it's your cup of tea, maybe it isn't.  If you don't enjoy what you're seeing in the first hour or so...the rest is more of the same so you'll have at least gotten that part sorted fairly quickly :D

Potions is a good game that has a lot of fun ideas. A potion dungeon crawler? Awesome! Fun story line following fairy tales and Asian folklore? Yup! Did I play this game all the way through because I enjoyed it? Of course! But the game falls short in some basic departments which would prevent me from recommending it to others: namely controls, settings, and quality of life.

The controls are fine. You use right click to fire potions, right click for everything else. However, it depends on a mouse. If you don't have one or can't use one, then tough luck. Potions can only be accessed using the number keys, where I would expect I could also scroll through my hotbar.

The settings are bare bones. You can change the windowed mode and the volume. However, I would expect more, such as being able to set frame rate, graphics quality, or remap my controls.

A few quality of life settings would make this game more enjoyable. For example, auto picking up items in chests instead of having to click on each drop to add them to my inventory. A mini map, showing what areas I've explored would also be really helpful. Being able to re-access tutorials would also be helpful, as once you click through it the mechanics are lost forever.

Other minor gripes include not seeing Old Haven develop (I bring people there, which unlocks small quests to get new potion recipes), no way to get hints or reminders about what I'm doing in a quest, and my frame rate really dropping on the lava levels. I also wasn't sure where I could fly over lava in the lava levels.

That being said, if you have it, do play it! I don't regret playing it. Just make sure that if you want to play it that you're aware of some of the shortcomings of the game in its current form.

I really wanted to like this game. I downloaded it after seeing the developer's video on TikTok. I think she mentioned it took 10 years to make, and the game sounded cozy with a slight challenge. I felt sympathy towards her so I wanted to try it out.

It is nothing like I expected. The game does NOT look or play like it took 10 years to make. Only being able to throw potions as a weapon would be okay if throwing potions could be sped up. I died a few times because I wasn't able to throw my potions fast enough. You can only carry a certain amount before you have to go back to grandma's house to brew and grab more. There are cauldrons in different areas of the game, but not nearly enough for how quickly I went through my potions. Sometimes I would brew a potion I thought I would need for a specific obstacle, but it turned out to be the wrong one... so back to grandma's I went to brew a new one and then had to walk all the way back to the area. This is another title I wish I could rate positively, but there are just a few too many frustrations to warrant.

I love the premise, the artwork is adorable, and I like the puzzle nature of things.  Where it falls apart is the combat, especially how the hitboxes work.

There are several required fights, with the large golems being the most visible of the issues.  Your only weapons are potions you make, which have different elements, different aoe types, and different damage values.  The problem is that you have a very long windup, and with how confusing the hitboxes of your character and the enemies are, it's likely you get hit before it goes off or you simply miss even though visually it should hit.  Getting hit is the same.  I had several hits, along with a death, caused by the golem hitting me when no part of its sprite was touching my character.

If you die, you lose all materials you have gathered since the last time you went home, along with all potions you have used.  While punishing, it wouldn't be bad if the hitboxes made sense.  Getting killed by what feels like cheap hits, only to have to re-grind up the rare materials you used is just added frustration.

Still, even though there's no trait system, this is probably the closest to a non-Gust Atelier game you can get.  Experimenting with the crafting is fun, trying out different things to get new materials is also fun.  I just wish the combat section and its frustrations weren't so bad so that I could enjoy the puzzle solving.

This game satisfies that part of my brain that wants to wander through the woods picking up random feathers, berries, and bits of string. The fact that there is a crafting system, Legend of Zelda like dungeon puzzles, and a plot is a sideshow to just exploring the environment. 

The core game mechanic is brewing potions, then using those potions to kill enemies and unlock new areas. Each potion takes 3 ingredients, so this game would be an unbearable slog if the developers had not provided means of mass collecting and mass brewing several things in a few clicks. 

Some new puzzles/enemies take the expenditure of several potions before a solution is found. Fortunately ingredients reset every time the player leaves and returns to an area. I eventually found areas that allowed me to quickly farm ingredients so I could keep the main potions in my arsenal well stocked.

Despite the game encouraging me to experiment to discover new potions there seemed to be no benefit to it, except filling every checkbox on a progress page. An explosion, or a water effect solves the same problem if it is tier 1 or tier 5. The combat never was so difficult as to warrant maxing out my gear.

While not being a groundbreaking experience in terms of visuals, plot, or mechanics I found this game well worth the time and money I spent on it.

Potions: A Curious Tale is a charming little adventure game. Little because it’s not long: it took me 10 hours of playtime to 100% it, but it was 10 hours that I enjoyed.

The game's core mechanic is very solid: you collect ingredients (be it from the environment or from monsters), which you can then use to craft various potions. These potions serve as your primary attack mechanic (against monsters to collect better ingredients and occasionally to fight against bosses) and are also key to solving a good portion of the game’s puzzles (which overall are fairly light in difficulties). The rest of the game you spent exploring the various locations, finding cards (that act as keys to unlock even more areas), and pursuing the storyline.

There is a lot of unexplored potential when it comes to the game’s core mechanics: with some 116 potion recipes, an immense number of potions do not serve a purpose in the game. Considering this, I say the game can use a DLC, expansion, or sequel with more complex puzzles and maps to utilize these recipes further.

There are several other minor areas that I think the game can use improvement on:
- Maybe I’m just a hoarder but I did not find the ingredient awards from the chests to be very rewarding: it might be better to replace several of them with potion recipes so that by the end of the game, the players would arrive organically closer to completing their recipe collection.
- There is a risk of the player getting stuck in the area to the top-left of Granny’s house when Wukong temporarily follows you. This was the only time I needed to reload the game over a bug.
- The game's stories are cute and serviceable, but some more depth would likely improve them. For example, a DLC/expansion/sequel storyline where you need to help the Prince can be a potential way to explore this.
- As a good number of the puzzles depend on having the right potions, not having them means you need to run back to a cauldron to (hopefully) procure the right potion. For the most part, this wasn’t a problem for me, but there were some instances where I needed to go back and forth. The cauldrons are placed at almost every cave, so they are not that infrequent, but nonetheless it would be nice if this hassle is resolved. Maybe the game can better hint at what potion will be needed (Helios can help with this for example), or in a future game, maybe Luna can get to carry a small alchemy kit and carry a limited number of ingredients to be able to brew potions while out and about.

A game addressed to adults, but clearly best suited as an educational puzzle game for children, Potions: A Curious Tale has a mixed reception.
 
Potions: A Curious Tale is a game on a complexity and difficulty for children and young teenagers. This fact is obscured by the odd marketing as a tough puzzle adventure. It is not a tough puzzle adventure if its hardest puzzle barely beats the first puzzle of a SNES Zelda game. The hardest riddles in the game are the number sorting puzzles for the temples and those start at 3 stages and end at 4. That is a small enough sample to brute force it quite easily. Although one can deduct which button is to be pressed first or last and then only brute force 1 to 2 steps if those puzzles are personally disliked.

If I had to judge this game under the premise of a grownup adventure puzzler, it would maybe reach a 5/10 due to a fair story, cute art and barebone puzzles and shallow alchemy. It's the story and aesthetic that saves it. It is worth its price, it just isn't for you likely. You will stop playing due to feeling like you play a children's game. Which based on achievements, most did around the spider forest and the first major boss "fight".

Thus I will try to be lenient and ignore the false marketing and judge this as a children's game. As a children's game it is quite good.

The puzzles have a difficulty curve, but it only increases a little over the game. The alchemy system is so basic, that it teaches children to combine number values to higher pairs for better potions. Some temples have "spatial intelligence" training, although you can just brute force until you find the right way. 

Most special riddles can be jumped with the broom which puts them ad absurdum. I feel the broom was a later addition and counters most puzzles. Which is good for children with little patience, but navigating a cave of falling stalactites or nail floors - or just using the broom speed to ignore it entirely - is not that difficult to begin with.

Some of the jokes are clearly grownup humor (Fire Fox being open source), but aside of the rather dark lore of the cards and our arrogant cannibal Baba Yaga, there is little dark motifs in this game. As such it is relatively safe to play, especially compared to really dark games like Voice of Cards. Those might traumatize your children.

It's okay. Buy it for your children. The price is fine too and a child will take more than 16 hours to finish this, a grown up will not, unless they lose patience and stumble around.

For adult people this is a 5/10
For children and teenager this is a 8/10
